before: In Africa my mother had been in the habit of bringing cakes, bread and wine to the churches built in memory of the saints. Once, when she did this, the doorkeeper stopped her. As soon as she learned that the bishop had forbidden it, she accepted his wish so devoutly and obediently that I myself was amazed at how readily she found fault with her own custom rather than argue about his ban. For no craving for wine laid siege to her spirit, and no love of wine goaded her into hating the truth, as it does to a great many men and women, who are sickened by any call to sobriety the way drunkards are sickened by a drink mixed with water. When she brought her basket of the customary festival food, to be tasted first by herself and then given away, she never set out more than one small cup of wine, diluted to suit her own very sober palate, from which she would take a sip for courtesy's sake. And if there were many shrines of the departed saints that seemed to deserve this kind of honor, she carried the same single cup around to set down at each. By then it was not only thoroughly watered but also unpleasantly lukewarm, and she would share it in tiny sips with those around her, because what she sought there was devotion, not pleasure. So when she discovered that this famous preacher and most devout bishop had ordered that it should not be done, even by those who did it soberly, so that no opening for gorging might be given to drunkards, and because these quasi-memorial feasts for the dead closely resembled the superstition of the pagans, she gave it up most willingly. In place of a basket full of the fruits of the earth, she had learned to bring to the shrines of the martyrs a heart full of purer prayers, and to give what she could to the poor. In this way the communion of the Lord's Body could be rightly celebrated in the place where the martyrs, in imitation of His Passion, were sacrificed and crowned. And yet it seems to me, O Lord my God, and this is how my heart judges it in Your sight, that perhaps she would not so easily have given up this custom if it had been forbidden by someone else whom she did not love as she loved Ambrose. She loved him dearly for the sake of my salvation, and he loved her for her deeply religious way of life, so fervent in spirit, as she went constantly to church doing good works. Often when he saw me he would break out in praise of her, congratulating me on having such a mother. He did not know what kind of son she had in me, a son who doubted all these things and did not believe the way of life could ever be found.
